sources.title: Linus Torvalds (Q34253) -- verified live via wbgetentities (2026-10-08): en label 'Linus Torvalds', description 'Finnish software engineer (born 1969)', born 28 Dec 1969, citizenship United States and Finland, instance of human. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'The Tanenbaum-Torvalds Debate' (comp.os.minix, 29 January - 10 February 1992), reproduced as Appendix A of Open Sources: Voices from the Open Source Revolution (O'Reilly, 1999) -- archived Usenet thread: Andrew Tanenbaum's 'LINUX is obsolete' post, Torvalds' replies and apology, and replies from third parties including Ken Thompson. ADVERSARIAL and first-hand; the book's editors add a framing note. Read in full for the Tanenbaum, Torvalds and Thompson posts; the long tail of third-party posts was skimmed.

Andrew Tanenbaum (Vrije Universiteit), 'Tanenbaum-Torvalds Debate Part II' -- the 2006 follow-up note by the adversary of the 1992 debate, stating that he has 'great respect' for what Torvalds accomplished and rejecting the claim that Linux was copied from MINIX. Read the preface and opening sections; the technical argument was skimmed.

Eric S. Raymond, 'The Cathedral and the Bazaar' (version 3.0), sections 'The Mail Must Get Through' and 'The Importance of Having Users', 'Release Early, Release Often' and 'How Many Eyeballs Tame Complexity' -- ADMIRING essayist's analysis of Torvalds' development style written from outside the kernel project (Raymond first met Linux in 1993). Read these sections in full; the remainder of the essay is about Raymond's own fetchmail project and was not read.

Linus Torvalds, 'LINUX's History' (written 31 July 1992), annotated collection of his own comp.os.minix posts of July-December 1991, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University -- SELF source (first-hand and retrospective). Read in full for the July-December 1991 posts and his notes on early release dates.

Linus Torvalds, linux-kernel mailing list post 'Re: GPL V3 and Linux - Dead Copyright Holders' (28 January 2006), Linux-Kernel Archive -- SELF source recalling the early kernel licence ('you may not distribute this for a fee') and its retroactive replacement by the GNU GPL. Read in full.

Linus Torvalds, linux-kernel mailing list post 'Linux 4.19-rc4 released, an apology, and a maintainership note' (16 September 2018), lkml archive at Indiana University -- SELF source: public apology for his earlier communication in kernel discussions, announcement that Greg Kroah-Hartman would finish the 4.19 release while he took a break. Read in full.

Noam Cohen, 'After Years of Abusive E-mails, the Creator of Linux Steps Aside', The New Yorker, 19 September 2018 -- INDEPENDENT investigative news report with interviews (Megan Squire, Sage Sharp, Valerie Aurora, Guido van Rossum) and statements relayed by the Linux Foundation; critical in framing. Read in full.

James Farrell, 'After meditating on his behavior, Linus Torvalds returns to Linux', SiliconANGLE, 23 October 2018 -- short news report on his return after the break, Greg Kroah-Hartman's handover message and the new code of conduct. Read in full.
Clare Hopping, 'Linus Torvalds returns to work on Linux development', IT Pro, 24 October 2018 -- short news report corroborating the return and the Kroah-Hartman handover. Read the main text.

Zack Brown, 'A Git Origin Story', Linux Journal, 27 July 2018 -- INDEPENDENT trade-press history by a long-time kernel-development chronicler (former author of Kernel Traffic): how kernel patches were handled before version control, the 2002 BitKeeper decision and its controversy, the 2005 loss of the free licence and Torvalds' creation of Git, and the hand-over of Git to Junio Hamano. Read in full.

Nathan Willis, 'BitKeeper goes open source', LWN.net, 11 May 2016 -- INDEPENDENT trade-press account of the BitKeeper licence dispute of 2005 and Git's origin, including competing positions of BitMover and Andrew Tridgell and Torvalds' public criticism of Tridgell. Read in full.

Jonathan Corbet, 'On the scalability of Linus', LWN.net, 2010 -- INDEPENDENT analysis by LWN's editor of the single-committer kernel model, the 1998 stoppage, later frustrations, and how BitKeeper and Git changed patch flow. Read in full.

Jonathan Corbet, 'What makes Linus happy (or not)?', LWN.net, 20 August 2014 -- INDEPENDENT report of Torvalds' own talk at the 2014 Kernel Summit on how he wants pull requests and regressions handled. Read in full.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_lt_tanenbaum, src_lt_raymond, src_lt_lj_git, src_lt_history1992 | 1991-2005 | archived adversarial Usenet thread + admiring essayist + trade-press history + self] In January 1992 an established operating-systems professor publicly called Linux's monolithic, 386-specific design obsolete; Torvalds, then a student, conceded microkernels were 'nicer' in theory but defended his design on what was available and working (his own posts), and Ken Thompson's reply in the thread called the design criterion largely unrelated to usefulness while agreeing microkernels were probably the future. In 2002-2005 Zack Brown reports he rejected CVS and Subversion and found none of the open-source distributed alternatives good enough, then wrote Git himself. Raymond describes his approach as 'conservative and simplifying' rather than a design leap, and notes the early reuse of Minix scaffolding, so the independence lies in choosing his own path against expert advice and available tools, not in conceptual novelty. Several dated instances across sources; capped below 75 because the 1992 position was defended in part by self posts and the technical question was later judged differently by the adversary himself (Part II).

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_lt_tanenbaum, src_lt_newyorker2018, src_lt_lwn_scale2010, src_lt_lkml2018 | 1992-2018 | archived adversarial thread + investigative news report + trade-press analysis + self] In January 1992 he answered Tanenbaum's public critique within hours with a deliberately combative post and apologised for its tone the next day. The New Yorker reports thousands of scathing public messages to kernel contributors over years, a researcher's tally of insults in a four-year sample of his mail, and his 2013 reply to Sage Sharp that he would not 'act professional' and that cursing was justified in some cases; former contributors told the reporter the style discouraged participation. His own 2018 post calls his past attacks unprofessional and uncalled for. LWN records that in 1998 he walked away from a dispute over dropped patches. dual_edged: willingness to stay in open, blunt disagreement, with documented costs to others. Score kept below 85 because the New Yorker's framing is critical and counts and tone come from a small number of reports.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_lt_history1992, src_lt_raymond, src_lt_lj_git | 1991-2005 | self + admiring essayist + trade-press history] His own dated posts show source releases 0.01 to 0.03 within about two months (September-October 1991, 'max 2-3 weeks' between releases). Raymond, an outside admirer, writes that around 1991 he sometimes released a new kernel more than once a day. Zack Brown reports Git was self-hosting within days of the June 2005 start, ready to host kernel development within weeks and fully functional within a couple of months, after which he handed it on. Speed is documented in three independent-in-time episodes; the Git timeline is a single trade-press retelling and its start date is disputed in other sources, hence moderate confidence.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_lt_history1992, src_lt_tanenbaum, src_lt_lj_git, src_lt_lwn_bk2016 | 1991-2005 | self + archived thread + trade-press history] In 1991 he started a kernel on his own machine because the GNU kernel was not ready (his Usenet reply of January 1992: 'If the GNU kernel had been ready last spring, I'd not have bothered'), posted publicly asking for feedback in August and invited others to take the sources in October. In April-June 2005, after BitMover withdrew the free licence, LWN and Linux Journal report he stopped kernel work and wrote his own version-control system rather than adopt an existing one. Two independently reported episodes of creating the missing tool himself; no rating from the outcome, only the pattern of acting on a gap.

collaboration.rationale: [src_lt_raymond, src_lt_lwn_scale2010, src_lt_lj_git, src_lt_lwn_happy2014 | 1991-2014 | admiring essayist + trade-press analysis + trade-press history + report of his own talk] Raymond describes him as treating users as co-developers and delegating widely; LWN describes a model in which subsystem maintainers feed work to him and he pulls from their trees; he handed Git's maintainership to Junio Hamano within months (Brown) and in 2014 told maintainers to respond quickly to their contributors (Corbet). The same sources describe a single point of final approval and, in the New Yorker, a communication style that drove some contributors away, so the score is moderate and dual_edged rather than high.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_lt_tanenbaum, src_lt_newyorker2018, src_lt_siliconangle2018, src_lt_lkml2018 | 1992 and 2013-2018 | archived thread + investigative report + news + self] The day after the 1992 flame exchange he posted an apology for his tone while still maintaining Linux was not obsolete. The New Yorker documents that until September 2018 he defended his abrasive style, including a 2013 public refusal to change it, and that he changed course after contributors confronted him: he posted a public apology, took a break, and a revised code of conduct was adopted; SiliconANGLE and IT Pro report he returned about a month later. A real but slow revision of one position, with the delay itself documented; kept near the middle.

provenance.notes: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-08) for Q34253: en label 'Linus Torvalds', description 'Finnish software engineer (born 1969)', born 28 Dec 1969, citizenship United States and Finland, human, no death date. SLUG CHECK: not in scratch/prod_slugs.txt, no existing candidate file. LIVING SUBJECT: only documented public professional behaviour used; no family, health or motive inference. The 2018 apology is cited from his own post and independent reporting and is used only for belief_updating and conflict_tolerance as a documented public event. CLASSIFICATION: occupation engineer (no computer_scientist: not an academic/research career); fields computing and technology (both have field.* keys); archetype technical_innovator (as larry-page, dennis-ritchie); tags innovator, leader. REGION: north_america chosen as the most honest existing code: dual Finnish-US citizenship (Wikidata), resident in the US since 1997 (New Yorker: lives outside Portland), same coding as other foreign-born US-career people (Alexander Graham Bell, Sikorsky); the Nordic-to-western_europe precedent was weighed because Linux was begun in Helsinki in 1991, so the lead may prefer western_europe. SOURCES READ: 14 records (13 substantive + 1 orientation): Tanenbaum-Torvalds 1992 thread (O'Reilly appendix), Tanenbaum Part II, Raymond's essay sections, Torvalds' 1992 history of his 1991 posts (CMU), Torvalds 2006 LKML GPL post, Torvalds' 2018 LKML apology, New Yorker 2018, SiliconANGLE 2018, IT Pro 2018, Linux Journal Git origin, LWN BitKeeper 2016, LWN scalability 2010, LWN 2014 summit. PERSPECTIVES: self (Torvalds' posts, never sole support); adversarial (Tanenbaum 1992, and his later respectful note); admiring (Raymond); independent journalism (New Yorker, LWN's Corbet and Willis, Linux Journal's Brown). NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL: New Yorker, LWN x3, Linux Journal, Raymond, Tanenbaum. NOT ACCESSED / NOT READ: Glyn Moody's Rebel Code (only the publisher page was reachable), Torvalds' book Just for Fun (not accessed), MIT Technology Review 'Linus's World' (page empty), the Wired and kernel.org pages (not found or not loaded), Greg Kroah-Hartman, Jon 'maddog' Hall and Bruce Perens interviews (not found); the Millennium Technology Prize 2012 was not sourced from a read page and is not used in the editorial or any row; the kernel documentation pages on pull requests and management style were only skimmed and no row rests on them. ROWS CONSIDERED AND LEFT UNSCORED: leadership_drive (final say is documented but no source read speaks to seeking the role; he wrote he hoped to skip the kernel summit), persuasiveness and social_assertiveness (overlap conflict_tolerance), autonomy_need and mastery_orientation (only his own 'hobby' posts), impact_motivation and achievement_drive (would rest on outcomes), systems_abstraction (Raymond says not a design leap), curiosity, empathy-related traits (not scored; no inference from his own 2018 self-description). Political/advocacy roles (GPL licensing debates) are not scored. PORTRAIT: Commons file page for the cropped file and its parent (own work of the uploader, dual CC BY-SA 3.0/4.0, Wikimedia Deutschland support template, permission ticket noted); no institutional rightsholder page conflicts.
